claim: High-speed atomic force microscopy was employed to observe structural changes in actin filaments induced by cofilin binding.
source: High-speed atomic force microscopy was employed to observe structural changes in actin filaments induced by cofilin binding.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the primary method used in the study.

claim: Cofilin formed clusters along actin filaments, where the filaments were 2-nm thicker compared to control filaments.
source: Consistent with previous electron and fluorescence microscopic studies, cofilin formed clusters along actin filaments, where the filaments were 2-nm thicker and the helical pitch was ∼25% shorter, compared to control filaments.
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the abstract and supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cofilin binding shortened the helical pitch by approximately 25% compared to control filaments.
source: Consistent with previous electron and fluorescence microscopic studies, cofilin formed clusters along actin filaments, where the filaments were 2-nm thicker and the helical pitch was ∼25% shorter, compared to control filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed by measurements in Figure 1E showing a reduction from 36.8 nm to 26.9 nm.

claim: The shortened helical pitch was propagated to the neighboring bare zone on the pointed-end side of the cluster.
source: Interestingly, the shortened helical pitch was propagated to the neighboring bare zone on the pointed-end side of the cluster, while the pitch on the barbed-end side was similar to the control.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The pitch on the barbed-end side of cofilin clusters was similar to the control.
source: Interestingly, the shortened helical pitch was propagated to the neighboring bare zone on the pointed-end side of the cluster, while the pitch on the barbed-end side was similar to the control.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements in Table 1.

claim: Cofilin clusters induce distinctively asymmetric conformational changes in filaments.
source: Thus, cofilin clusters induce distinctively asymmetric conformational changes in filaments.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract based on the observed differences in helical pitch on either side of cofilin clusters.

claim: Cofilin favors actin structures with a shorter helical pitch.
source: Consistent with the idea that cofilin favors actin structures with a shorter helical pitch, cofilin clusters grew unidirectionally toward the pointed-end of the filament.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the observed unidirectional growth pattern.

claim: Cofilin clusters grew unidirectionally toward the pointed-end of the filament.
source: Consistent with the idea that cofilin favors actin structures with a shorter helical pitch, cofilin clusters grew unidirectionally toward the pointed-end of the filament.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by observations in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Severing was often observed near the boundaries between bare zones and clusters.
source: Severing was often observed near the boundaries between bare zones and clusters, but not necessarily at the boundaries.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: Severing was not necessarily observed at the boundaries between bare zones and clusters.
source: Severing was often observed near the boundaries between bare zones and clusters, but not necessarily at the boundaries.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the distribution of severing events shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Actin filaments are involved in muscle contraction, amoeboid movement, cytokinesis, intracellular transport, and transcriptional regulation within the nucleus.
source: Actin filaments are involved in a variety of important functions in eukaryotic cells, including muscle contraction, amoeboid movement, cytokinesis, intracellular transport, and transcriptional regulation within the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about actin functions.

claim: Cofilin plays essential roles in continuous extension of lamellipodia by severing actin filaments to promote filament depolymerization or to initiate polymerization from new barbed ends.
source: During migration of amoeboid cells, for instance, cofilin plays essential roles in continuous extension of lamellipodia by severing actin filaments to promote filament depolymerization or to initiate polymerization from new barbed ends (reviewed by Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Three independent biochemical mechanisms are known to inhibit cofilin activity: phosphorylation of Ser3, sequestration to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in plasma membrane, and lower pH.
source: Three independent biochemical mechanisms are known to inhibit cofilin activity; phosphorylation of Ser3, sequestration to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in plasma membrane, and lower pH (Bernstein and Bamburg, 2010; Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active S3A cofilin did not inhibit motility.
source: Indeed, overexpression of constitutively active S3A cofilin did not inhibit motility (Endo et al., 2003; Popow-Wozniak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Biochemical signaling is not sufficient to explain how cofilin activities are properly regulated spatially and temporally in cells.
source: Thus, biochemical signaling is not sufficient to explain how cofilin activities are properly regulated spatially and temporally in cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the introduction based on the cited evidence about S3A cofilin.

claim: Dense binding of cofilin shortens the helical pitch of actin filaments by 25%.
source: In addition, dense binding of cofilin shortens the helical pitch of actin filaments by 25% (McGough et al., 1997; Galkin et al., 2001; Sharma et al., 2011), and time-resolved phosphorescence anisotropy (Prochniewicz et al., 2005) and differential scanning calorimetry (Dedova et al., 2004; Bobkov et al., 2006) showed that one molecule of bound cofilin changes the structure of ∼100 actin subunits within a filament.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: One molecule of bound cofilin changes the structure of approximately 100 actin subunits within a filament.
source: In addition, dense binding of cofilin shortens the helical pitch of actin filaments by 25% (McGough et al., 1997; Galkin et al., 2001; Sharma et al., 2011), and time-resolved phosphorescence anisotropy (Prochniewicz et al., 2005) and differential scanning calorimetry (Dedova et al., 2004; Bobkov et al., 2006) showed that one molecule of bound cofilin changes the structure of ∼100 actin subunits within a filament.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to biophysical studies.

claim: Binding of cofilin to actin filaments is cooperative.
source: Moreover, binding of cofilin to actin filaments is cooperative (Hawkins et al., 1993; Hayden et al., 1993; McGough et al., 1997; De La Cruz, 2005; Hayakawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Right-handed double helical filaments were clearly visualized using HS-AFM.
source: Right-handed double helical filaments were clearly visualized (Figure 1), as in earlier reports (Weisenhorn et al., 1990; Schmitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1 and citations to earlier AFM studies.

claim: The thickness of control actin filaments was 8.6 ± 0.8 nm.
source: Quantitative analysis indicated that the height of those peaks, or the thickness of the filaments, was 8.6 ± 0.8 nm (average ± SD), and the spacing between the peaks, or half helical pitch, was 36.8 ± 4.3 nm (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The half helical pitch of control actin filaments was 36.8 ± 4.3 nm.
source: Quantitative analysis indicated that the height of those peaks, or the thickness of the filaments, was 8.6 ± 0.8 nm (average ± SD), and the spacing between the peaks, or half helical pitch, was 36.8 ± 4.3 nm (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The measured values of filament thickness and half helical pitch are consistent with previously reported structural data.
source: These values, which are consistent with previously reported structural data (Hanson and Lowy, 1963; Hanson, 1973; Egelman et al., 1982), will hereafter be referred to as normal height and normal half helical pitch, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to earlier structural studies.

claim: The distribution of half helical pitches ranged from approximately 26 nm to approximately 45 nm.
source: The distribution of half helical pitches ranged from ∼26 nm to ∼45 nm and was well fit by a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 4.3 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on measurements from AFM images.

claim: The distribution of half helical pitches was well fit by a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 4.3 nm.
source: The distribution of half helical pitches ranged from ∼26 nm to ∼45 nm and was well fit by a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 4.3 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis of the measurements.

claim: Actin filament paracrystals were prepared in the presence of 30 mM MgCl2.
source: To assess the overall magnitude of the measurement errors, we prepared paracrystals of actin filaments in the presence of 30 mM MgCl2 (Figure 1C) (Hanson, 1973).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C, with a citation to the method.

claim: The distribution of half helical pitches of paracrystals had a mean of 36.5 nm and standard deviation of 3.0 nm.
source: The distribution of the half helical pitches of the paracrystals measured under the same conditions was narrower than that of free filaments, with a mean of 36.5 nm and standard deviation of 3.0 nm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Peak heights within long cofilin clusters showed a single distribution of 10.6 nm ± 1.0 nm, approximately 2 nm taller than the control filaments.
source: Peak heights within long cofilin clusters (longer than eight consecutive half helices) showed a single distribution of 10.6 nm ± 1.0 nm, approximately 2 nm taller than the control filaments (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The increased height of cofilin-decorated filaments is consistent with electron microscopic analysis showing filaments fully decorated with cofilin are approximately 2.3-nm thicker than control filaments.
source: This is consistent with electron microscopic analysis (Galkin et al., 2011), which showed that filaments fully decorated with cofilin are ∼2.3-nm thicker than control filaments due to the presence of cofilin molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within long cofilin clusters, both actin strands are homogeneously bound with cofilin molecules.
source: Moreover, the height distribution was fit well by a single normal distribution, which suggests that within those long cofilin clusters, both actin strands are homogeneously bound with cofilin molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the height distribution is fit by a single normal distribution.

claim: Cofilin binding shortened the half helical pitch by 27% to 26.9 nm.
source: Cofilin binding shortened the half helical pitch by 27% to 26.9 nm (Figure 1E), which is again consistent with earlier electron microscopic (McGough et al., 1997; Galkin et al., 2001) and AFM analyses (Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1E and citations to previous studies.

claim: The standard deviation of the distribution of half helical pitches of fully cofilin-decorated filaments was 3.8 nm.
source: The standard deviation of the distribution of half helical pitches of the fully cofilin-decorated filaments was 3.8 nm, and subtracting the maximum possible measurement error yielded a standard deviation of 2.3 nm or larger.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis of measurements.

claim: Cofilin binding restricts torsional movements of the filaments within cofilin clusters.
source: This value is smaller than that of the control filaments (3.1 nm) and suggests that cofilin binding restricts torsional movements of the filaments within cofilin clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of standard deviations between control and cofilin-decorated filaments.

claim: The half helical pitch in the apparently bare section on the pointed-end side of the cofilin cluster was short.
source: This analysis revealed that the half helical pitch of the bare zone on the pointed-end side of the cofilin cluster was short, while that on the barbed-end side was slightly longer than the normal pitch (Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The half helical pitch on the barbed-end side of cofilin clusters was slightly longer than the normal pitch.
source: This analysis revealed that the half helical pitch of the bare zone on the pointed-end side of the cofilin cluster was short, while that on the barbed-end side was slightly longer than the normal pitch (Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The differences in the mean half helical pitches between the first neighbor bare zone on either side of the cluster and the control filaments are statistically significant.
source: Student's t-test indicated that the differences in the mean half helical pitches between the first neighbor bare zone on either side of the cluster and the control filaments are statistically significant (p < 0.00001 and p < 0.001 for pointed-end and barbed-end side, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: Pitches of the neighboring half helices second from the cofilin clusters were nearly normal.
source: Pitches of the neighboring half helices second from the cofilin clusters were nearly normal (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: A cofilin-rod fusion protein was engineered with the N-terminal half of the rod domain of α-actinin attached to the C-terminus of cofilin.
source: We therefore engineered a fusion protein in which the N-terminal half of the rod domain of α-actinin was attached to the C-terminus of cofilin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: Clusters of cofilin-rod showed a half helical pitch approximately 25% shorter than the bare zones, similar to control cofilin molecules bound to actin filaments.
source: In electron micrographs of negatively stained specimens (Figure 3A), as well as in HS-AFM images (Video 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), we were able to see clusters of cofilin-rod with a half helical pitch ∼25% shorter than the bare zones, which is similar to control cofilin molecules bound to actin filaments (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3A, Video 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Rod-like structures observed sticking out from apparently bare sections of filaments are most likely the rod portions of cofilin-rod molecules bound sparsely along the filaments.
source: Rod-like structures were often observed to stick out from apparently bare sections of the filaments (Figure 3B). These are most likely the rod portions of the cofilin-rod molecules bound sparsely along seemingly bare sections of the filaments, because their length was ∼10 nm, which is expected for half an α-actinin rod (Yan et al., 1993; Anson et al., 1996), and because similar rod-like structures were rarely observed in control images of cofilin added to actin filaments (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3B, Figure 3C, and citations about rod length.

claim: The helical pitches around apparently singly bound cofilin-rod molecules did not significantly differ from the control helical pitch measured in electron micrographs.
source: Furthermore, the helical pitches around the apparently singly bound cofilin-rod molecules (36.0 ± 1.0 nm, n = 5) did not significantly differ from the control helical pitch (36.3 ± 1.0 nm, n = 8) measured in electron micrographs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on measurements from electron micrographs.

claim: A single cofilin molecule cannot induce conformational changes that involve detectable changes in helical pitch when it binds to bare sections of the filament.
source: These results suggest that a single cofilin molecule cannot induce conformational changes, either symmetric or asymmetric, that involve detectable changes in helical pitch when it binds to bare sections of the filament.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the observations of singly bound cofilin-rod.

claim: Real time AFM imaging taken at 1.5 or 2 frames/s enabled following the growth of individual cofilin clusters along actin filaments.
source: Real time AFM imaging taken at 1.5 or 2 frames/s enabled us to follow the growth of individual cofilin clusters along actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental capability.

claim: The directional growth of cofilin clusters toward the pointed-end was observed in actin filaments with homogenous nucleotide states.
source: HS-AFM observations after the addition of 20 nM S1 and 75 nM cofilin or 150 nM S1 and 900 nM cofilin demonstrated that, in both cases, the growth of cofilin clusters was primarily to the pointed-end direction (Figure 4B and Video 4, and Figure 4C and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figures 4B, 4C, Videos 4 and 5.

claim: Cofilin binds preferentially to actin subunits carrying ADP, compared to those carrying ATP or ADP and Pi.
source: Cofilin binds preferentially to actin subunits carrying ADP, compared to those carrying ATP or ADP and Pi (Carlier et al., 1997; Blanchoin and Pollard, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: The rate of formation and growth of cofilin clusters depended on the nucleotide state of actin subunits as well as the concentration of cofilin.
source: The rate of formation and growth of cofilin clusters depended on the nucleotide state of actin subunits as well as the concentration of cofilin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations under different conditions.

claim: Severing was often observed between 40 and 200 nM cofilin.
source: Severing was often observed between 40 (Video 12 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and 200 nM cofilin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 12 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Approximately 60% of severing events occurred inside the cofilin clusters, mostly within half helices neighboring bare zones.
source: Approximately 60% of severing events occurred inside the cofilin clusters, mostly within half helices neighboring bare zones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative analysis of severing positions.

claim: Severing also occurred in half helices in bare zones neighboring a cofilin cluster, which accounted for approximately 40% of severing events.
source: Severing also occurred in half helices in bare zones neighboring a cofilin cluster, which accounted for approximately 40% of severing events.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative analysis.

claim: Overall, approximately 80% of the severing events occurred within one-half of a helix on either side of the boundary between a bare zone and a cofilin cluster.
source: Overall, ∼80% of the severing events occurred within one-half of a helix on either side of the boundary between a bare zone and a cofilin cluster.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative analysis of severing positions.

claim: Severing in bare zones far from cofilin clusters was very rare.
source: Severing in bare zones far from cofilin clusters was very rare.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations.

claim: Severing under the present experimental condition preferentially occurs near the boundary between a bare zone and a cofilin cluster, but not necessarily at the boundary.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that severing under the present experimental condition preferentially occurs near the boundary between a bare zone and a cofilin cluster, but not necessarily at the boundary.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the severing data.

claim: The conclusion about severing location is consistent with that made by Suarez et al. (2011) using fluorescence microscopy.
source: Considering the difference in spatial resolution, this conclusion is also consistent with that made by Suarez et al. (2011), who used fluorescence microscopy and concluded that severing occurs at the boundary between cofilin clusters and bare zones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the current findings with previous work.

claim: The fact that actin filaments are not necessarily free to rotate in vivo suggests similar passive untwisting may occur in vivo as well.
source: If that is the case, the fact that actin filaments are not necessarily free to rotate in vivo suggests similar passive untwisting may occur in vivo as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of passive untwisting mechanisms.

claim: Propagation of the supertwisted conformation from cofilin clusters to neighbor bare zones had been suggested by image analysis of electron micrographs of cofilin–actin complexes.
source: Propagation of the supertwisted conformation from cofilin clusters to neighbor bare zones had been suggested by image analysis of electron micrographs of cofilin–actin complexes (Galkin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: The observation that cofilin clusters grew in the pointed-end direction supports the conclusion of Galkin et al. (2001) that cofilin preferentially binds to the supertwisted segments of actin subunits.
source: Our observation that the cofilin clusters grew in the pointed-end direction supports the conclusion of Galkin et al. (2001) that cofilin preferentially binds to the supertwisted segments of actin subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section connecting the current findings to previous work.

claim: The directional growth of cofilin clusters does not depend on a gradient of different nucleotide states on actin subunits within each filament.
source: This tendency of cofilin clusters to grow unidirectionally was unaffected when most of the filament subunits carried ADP or ADP+Pi, demonstrating that the directional growth of cofilin clusters does not depend on a gradient of different nucleotide states on actin subunits within each filament.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on experiments with different nucleotide conditions.

claim: The directional growth of cofilin clusters presumably depends on asymmetric cofilin-induced conformational changes in the actin filaments, which is an intrinsic property of the polar structure of the actin filaments.
source: Instead, it presumably depends on asymmetric cofilin-induced conformational changes in the actin filaments, which is an intrinsic property of the polar structure of the actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Previous biochemical and simulation studies suggested that one or a few bound cofilin molecules are sufficient to sever actin filaments.
source: Previous biochemical (Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006) and simulation studies (De La Cruz, 2005; De La Cruz, 2009) suggested that one or a few bound cofilin molecules are sufficient to sever actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The AFM observations are more consistent with the view that efficient severing requires a cofilin cluster longer than one-half of a helix.
source: However, our AFM observations are more consistent with the view that efficient severing requires a cofilin cluster longer than one-half of a helix, since most of the severing events were observed within or very near cofilin clusters that were recognizable in our AFM images.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the severing observations.

claim: The need of contiguously bound cofilin molecules for efficient severing is consistent with earlier mutant analysis.
source: The need of contiguously bound cofilin molecules for efficient severing is consistent with our earlier mutant analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section connecting to previous work by the authors.

claim: Cofilin was able to bind to copolymers of D11Q and wild-type actins, but severing was inefficient.
source: Interestingly, cofilin was able to bind to copolymers of D11Q and wild-type actins, but severing was inefficient (Umeki et al., 2012), suggesting that contiguous clusters of cofilin-bound actin subunits are necessary for efficient severing activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Previous simulation studies suggested that two cofilin molecules bound close to one another along an actin filament serve as a nucleus to initiate cooperative binding of cofilin to form a cluster.
source: Consistent with this view, previous simulation studies suggested that two cofilin molecules bound close to one another along an actin filament serve as a nucleus to initiate cooperative binding of cofilin to form a cluster (Ressad et al., 1998; Blanchoin and Pollard, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to simulation studies.

claim: Cofilin is able to induce at least two distinct types of cooperative conformational changes.
source: Apparently cofilin is able to induce at least two distinct types of cooperative conformational changes: one that requires cluster formation, involves ∼25% supertwisting of the helix, and propagates over half a helix toward the pointed-end of the filament; and a second type that singly bound cofilin molecules can induce which involves relatively subtle conformational changes, and propagates much longer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a synthesis of the findings.

claim: Simulation studies by De La Cruz and Sept (2010) suggest that there are two distinct states of cofilin–actin complexes.
source: Simulation studies by De La Cruz and Sept (2010) suggest that there are two distinct states of cofilin–actin complexes, which may be correlated with the two types of cooperative conformational changes we propose here.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to a simulation study.

claim: Cooperativity in the binding of cofilin to actin filaments could amplify small changes in the input (concentration of active cofilin) to a larger difference in output (cluster formation and severing).
source: Generally speaking, cooperativity would amplify small changes in the input (concentration of active cofilin) to a larger difference in output (cluster formation and severing).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a general principle about cooperativity.

claim: The cellular concentration of cofilin is lower than that of polymerized actin.
source: In addition, the cellular concentration of cofilin is lower than that of polymerized actin, and cooperativity would be a useful means of disrupting selected filaments under those conditions (Pollard et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Tropomyosin inhibits binding of cofilin and protects the filaments from cofilin's severing and depolymerizing activities.
source: However, those actin filaments are often bound with tropomyosin (Gunning et al., 2008), which inhibits binding of cofilin and protects the filaments from cofilin's severing and depolymerizing activities (Bernstein and Bamburg, 1982; Ono and Ono, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: If cofilin forms a small cluster at a vacant site on an actin filament that is otherwise decorated and protected by tropomyosin, the cluster would induce supertwisting on the neighboring tropomyosin-bound segment on the pointed-end side.
source: If cofilin forms a small cluster at a vacant site on an actin filament that is otherwise decorated and protected by tropomyosin, the cluster would induce, or apply conformational stress to induce, supertwisting on the neighboring tropomyosin-bound segment on the pointed-end side.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Supertwisting would accelerate dissociation of tropomyosin, resulting in faster growth of the cofilin cluster than when cluster growth needed to wait for spontaneous dissociation of neighboring tropomyosin molecules.
source: This would accelerate dissociation of tropomyosin, resulting in faster growth of the cofilin cluster than when cluster growth needed to wait for spontaneous dissociation of neighboring tropomyosin molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Within cells, formin remains bound to the barbed-end when it catalyzes filament elongation, causing relative rotation between the formin molecule and the filament.
source: Within cells, formin remains bound to the barbed-end when it catalyzes filament elongation. This causes relative rotation between the formin molecule and the filament (Mizuno et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: If the formin molecule and the filament are not free to rotate, the filament will be untwisted, and if cofilin has a lower affinity for untwisted actin filaments, rapidly polymerizing actin filaments in a formin-dependent manner will be protected from severing by cofilin.
source: Thus, if the formin molecule and the filament are not free to rotate, the filament will be untwisted, and if cofilin has a lower affinity for untwisted actin filaments, rapidly polymerizing actin filaments in a formin-dependent manner will be protected from severing by cofilin (Mizuno and Watanabe, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Formin bound to the barbed-end of an actin filament also allosterically changes the structure of the filament, which may interfere with the interactions of the filament with cofilin, independent of mechanically forced untwisting of the filament helix.
source: It should be noted, however, that formin bound to the barbed-end of an actin filament also allosterically changes the structure of the filament (Bugyi et al., 2006), which may interfere with the interactions of the filament with cofilin, independent of mechanically forced untwisting of the filament helix.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Sharma et al. (2012) discovered that the untwisted conformation of actin filaments induced by a drebrin N-terminal fragment propagates to neighboring bare zones.
source: Sharma et al. (2012) discovered that the untwisted conformation of actin filaments induced by a drebrin N-terminal fragment propagates to neighboring bare zones; however, their findings seem to indicate that this propagation is in both directions from the drebrin clusters, though the authors did not address that point.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: There are multiple forms of ABP-induced cooperative conformational changes to actin filaments that propagate into bare zones.
source: It thus appears that there are multiple forms of ABP-induced cooperative conformational changes to actin filaments that propagate into bare zones, which implies there are also multiple physiological functions for such cooperative conformational changes to actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on comparison with other studies.

claim: cDNA encoding human cofilin 1 was amplified from a human cDNA library using PCR.
source: cDNA encoding human cofilin 1 was amplified from a human cDNA library using PCR with primers 5′-ggtaccatggcctccggtgt and 5′-tctagacaaaggcttgccctcca.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: The first half of the Dictyostelium α-actinin rod, corresponding to amino acid residues 265–505 of the parent molecule, forms a monomeric 12-nm long rod-like structure.
source: The first half of the Dictyostelium α-actinin rod, corresponding to amino acid residues 265–505 of the parent molecule, forms a monomeric12-nm long rod-like structure (Yan et al., 1993) and has been used as an artificial lever arm of myosin motors (Anson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations.

claim: Cofilin with and without His-tag bound to actin filaments at a 1:1 molar ratio with a similar affinity.
source: Cofilin with and without His-tag bound to actin filaments at a 1:1 molar ratio with a similar affinity (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Cofilin-rod with and without His-tag did not sediment on its own, then bound to actin filaments with affinities similar to cofilin without the rod fusion.
source: Cofilin-rod with and without His-tag also did not sediment on its own, then bound to actin filaments with affinities similar to cofilin without the rod fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A laboratory built high-speed atomic force microscope (HS-AFM) was used for imaging.
source: We used a laboratory built high-speed atomic force microscope (HS-AFM) as described previously (Ando et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation.

claim: HS-AFM imaging was carried out in the tapping mode with small cantilevers.
source: HS-AFM imaging was carried out in the tapping mode with small cantilevers (BL-AC10DS-A2, Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) whose spring constant, resonant frequency in water, and quality factor in water were ∼0.10 N/m, ∼400 kHz, and ∼2, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the experimental setup.

claim: Small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) and mica-supported lipid bilayer were prepared as described previously.
source: We prepared small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) and mica-supported lipid bilayer as described previously (Yamamoto et al., 2010; Uchihashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations.

claim: The typical lipid composition was DPPC and DPTAP at a weight ratio of 9:1.
source: The typical lipid composition was 1,2-dipamitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DPPC) and 1,2-dipalmitoyl-3-trimethylammonium-propane (DPTAP) at a weight ratio of 9:1.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the experimental materials.
